newsitem.title: USA: US Supreme Court hears Alaska submerged lands case.
newsitem.headline: US Supreme Court hears Alaska submerged lands case.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments on Monday on whether the state of Alaska or the federal government owns environmentally-sensitive submerged lands off the state's Arctic Coast that may hold oil.
The U.S. government claimed it retained certain submerged lands off the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and the National Petroleum Reserve, both federal lands.

But the state said the U.S. government did not go through proper procedures to keep those lands and so they became Alaska's under a law that grants coastal states title to submerged lands extending three miles out to sea.

Environmental groups, backing the federal government, fear that Alaska would promote oil production along the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coast, which they said would imperil wildlife and ruin the pristine wilderness.
Also at stake is $1.4 billion in oil and natural gas lease bids from the NPR coastal area which has been put in escrow until the case is decided.
The case, involving arcane land conveyance laws and deciding what constitutes an island, started in 1979 when the federal government filed a high court request to bring the complaint.

The state did not oppose the move, and the court named a special judicial officer, who held years of hearings and inquiries and issued a report in March that said the federal government had not "withdrawn or otherwise set apart" the submerged lands off ANWR as wildlife refuge.

The justices, who are to decide the case by the end of June, raised questions on whether the special judicial officer's interpretations raised questions on ownership of ANWR's uplands as well as barrier islands and submerged lands.
Arguing for the federal government, Jeffrey Minear, assistant to the solicitor general, said the interpretation "raises serious questions."
But attorney Thomas Koester, arguing for the state, said Alaska never had claim to the uplands in the wildlife refuge, and said he would urge Alaska not to contest ownership of the uplands.
The special judicial officer found that the federal government had claimed submerged lands in the petroleum reserve.

Koester said there was no congressional action to retain the submerged lands, but Minear said Congress took that action by passing the Submerged Lands Act which provided that coastal states do not take title to lands "expressly retained by...the United States."
Minear also said if Congress decided it did not intend to retain the submerged lands, the federal government could convey them to the states.
